# SPARC - Symbiotic Partners of Asgard Research Cruise

[SPARC](https://schmidtocean.org/cruise/searching-for-the-asgard/) was a 2025 research expedition aboard the [Schmidt Ocean Institute's R/V Falkor (too)](https://schmidtocean.org/) led by Drs. Brett Baker and Alyson Santoro. The expedition explored waters off Uruguay in search of living Asgard archaea, a group of microorganisms considered the closest known archaeal relatives of eukaryotes, and their potential bacterial partners. By studying these organisms, the team hoped to better understand how complex life evolved from simpler cells.

<center><iframe width="560" height="315" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/Jy_boPdY0zo?si=RoROTZkBKWxXYgZt" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture" allowfullscreen></iframe></center>

The origin of the first eukaryotic cell remains one of biology's biggest unsolved questions. Genomic evidence suggests that Asgard archaea share important cellular features with eukaryotes, offering clues about the organisms and evolutionary processes involved in eukaryogenesis. One leading hypothesis proposes that eukaryotes arose through a close association between an archaeal host and a bacterial partner. During SPARC, the team focused in part on identifying Hodarchaeales, an Asgard lineage potentially associated with coastal sediments influenced by freshwater and seawater mixing, including those near the mouth of Uruguay's Río de la Plata.

Working with the Santoro Lab, Dr. Jason Graff used cell-sorting flow cytometry to isolate and purify archaeal cells for downstream cultivation and sequencing efforts.

We also took advantage of the expedition to advance our [PACE Validation Science Team research](https://nbaetge.github.io/pvst.html). A substantial portion of our shipboard work focused on collecting biological, biogeochemical, and bio-optical measurements to evaluate relationships between ocean color observations and underlying biological processes. These included measurements relevant to phytoplankton biomass, particulate organic carbon, and ocean optical properties, helping expand PACE validation observations into the productive and dynamic waters of the southwestern Atlantic.

Read more about our work off the coast of Urugauy from Dr. Graff's NASA [Notes from the Field](https://science.nasa.gov/blogs/notes-from-the-field/2026/04/27/off-uruguay-pace-partners-connect-data-from-satellite-and-sea/).

The SPARC expedition also inspired creative collaborations beyond the research vessel. Uruguayan journalist Inés helped organize a musical project featuring several renowned Uruguayan artists, with a song inspired in part by our expedition. The accompanying music video includes footage from our time at sea, offering a beautiful connection between ocean exploration, music, and the communities that helped bring this expedition to life.
